report.name: Database Resource Usage
report.description: Who consumes the machine NOW and over time: live rates for the last minute (instance) and last ~15 seconds (per session), the SQL active in the last 30 minutes, then CPU, memory (PGA), disk I/O, logical reads and network per session, user and machine, plus the lifetime heaviest SQL. RAC-aware (all GV$). The live-rate sections answer 'what is loading the box right now'; session/user counters are cumulative since logon — read them together.
report.analysis_instructions:
IDIOMA: escreva TODO o relatório em português (pt-BR). Não traduza jargão técnico consagrado (session, logical reads, buffer gets, PGA, wait class, SQL*Net etc.).

The line above defines the report's OUTPUT LANGUAGE. EVERYTHING is written in that language: prose, table headers, fixed labels and section titles. English titles/labels in this specification are meant to be TRANSLATED, never copied. Numbering, order and meaning never change.

This report answers two questions: what is loading the machine RIGHT NOW, and who consumes it over time — CPU, memory (PGA), disk I/O, logical reads, network — by session, user and machine, plus the heaviest SQL. Every query is GV$ (RAC-aware): on a multi-instance database each table already carries inst_id, so always report which INSTANCE a consumer is on. Each query's description starts with a tag [1]-[9] naming its section.

TWO KINDS OF NUMBERS — state the difference and honour it:
- LIVE RATES: the instance rates (gv$sysmetric, last ~60s) and the per-session rates (gv$sessmetric, last ~15s) measure the PRESENT. When the trigger is a load ticket ("the server is slow NOW"), the reading order is: live instance rates → live session rates → active snapshot → recently-active SQL. These sections name the current offenders.
- CUMULATIVE: the per-session and per-user counters (CPU, logical reads, physical bytes, SQL*Net bytes) are CUMULATIVE SINCE LOGON — lifetime totals, not rates. A session connected for days outranks one briefly heavy. Never call a cumulative leader a "current problem" unless the live tables confirm it; a cumulative giant absent from the live tables is history and attribution, not the present. PGA (Top Sessions by Memory) and the active snapshot are live; Top SQL totals are cumulative since each cursor loaded.

PRECISION RULES (each exists because a real run got it wrong):
- Every result table is sorted by ONE column (named in its description). Before claiming "the largest/heaviest by X", RE-RANK the rows by column X yourself — the table's order proves nothing about any other column.
- Link a session to a SQL statement ONLY when a result of this run shows that sql_id on that session (live rates, active detail or PGA table). A parsing schema that merely matches the session's user is circumstantial — you may mention it, but call it circumstantial, never "strongly associated".
- A session whose program is the BHTDB.ai app itself is THIS TOOL's own connection, collecting this report — it WILL appear in the live-rate tables because collecting is work. Identify it as such and discount it; never present the tool as a finding.
- Copy identifiers and figures character-for-character from the result tables: inst_id:sid, serial#, sql_id, user, machine and every number. Never cite a sid or a value that does not appear in a result, and keep the same session's identifier consistent across sections. Name the database edition exactly as the environment states it — never reword it.
- In Top SQL, disk_reads and buffer_gets are BLOCKS, not bytes — convert with the block size only if you know it, otherwise compare in blocks.

FORMAT (Markdown) — built to be scanned, not just read:
- Each section title is a level-2 heading ("## 1. …"), title text in the output language. Blank line between every title, paragraph, list and table.
- Sections 2 to 9 OPEN with a COMPACT Markdown table holding only the rows you actually discuss (3 to 8 rows, never more — the full data is already attached to the report), with short headers in the output language. For session sections: session (inst:sid), user, machine/program, plus that section's metric column(s). For Top SQL: sql_id, schema, executions and the key costs. Always complete Markdown syntax: header row, |---| separator line, one row per line.
- BELOW each table, a SHORT reading — 2 to 4 sentences naming the leader and what the numbers mean. The prose must ADD meaning (context, cross-reference, caveat), never restate every number already visible in the table above it.
- Section 1 is the exception: a short executive paragraph a manager could read (include the live rates verdict: is the box under pressure right now, yes or no, and from what), plus the per-instance table when there is more than one instance.
- Bold the ONE number that matters most in each section's reading.
- Large byte values in MB or GB (say which); use the output language's digit grouping consistently in prose and tables.
- If a section has nothing noteworthy, say so in one line — analyzed, nothing stands out — with no empty table.

1. Load Overview (Portuguese title: Panorama de Carga) — open with the LIVE verdict from the instance rates (host CPU %, average active sessions, I/O and network per second): is the machine under pressure right now and from what. Then the per-instance overview (on RAC, which node is hot) and the live active picture (active sessions by resource class; Idle-class waiters are already excluded by the query).

2. Live Session Rates (Portuguese title: Consumo ao Vivo por Sessão) — the last ~15 seconds per session: who is consuming NOW (CPU seconds in the interval, logical reads, physical read MB, PGA), with their current sql_id. This section, not the cumulative ones, names the current offenders; cross their sql_id with section 9's recently-active list. If the table is EMPTY and the connection is a PDB, state that Oracle does not populate per-session metrics inside a PDB and answer "who is heavy now" from the active-sessions snapshot (who is ACTIVE, sql_running_since) plus the recently-active Top SQL (users_executing) — do not treat the empty table as "nobody is consuming".

3. CPU (title stays "CPU") — the top CUMULATIVE CPU consumers since logon (and which users/machines from section 8). Name inst:sid, user, machine and the CPU seconds; say explicitly whether each leader also appears in the live tables (current) or not (historical).

4. Memory / PGA (Portuguese title: Memória / PGA) — the PGA consumers (live) and the instance PGA overview. The overview is cumulative SINCE INSTANCE STARTUP: "over allocation count" counts times the instance was forced to allocate MORE than the target (untunable demand) — it is NOT temp spill; actual spill shows as "extra bytes read/written" versus "bytes processed" (the cache hit % summarizes them). A high historical counter alongside an excellent current hit % supports "consider raising the target", never "proven current crisis". Name the biggest pga_alloc_mb sessions and what they run.

5. Disk I/O (Portuguese title: I/O de Disco) — the sessions with the most physical read/write MB (cumulative), and the SQL behind them (respect the session↔SQL evidence rule). Real disk traffic is the scarcest resource; lead with it when it is high.

6. Logical Reads (title stays "Logical Reads") — the biggest buffer-gets sessions: CPU/cache pressure, usually a plan doing far more work than needed. Tie to Top SQL by gets/exec.

7. Network (Portuguese title: Rede) — sessions shipping the most SQL*Net bytes; a large sent volume points at unfiltered/unpaginated result sets.

8. By User and by Machine (Portuguese title: Por Usuário e por Máquina) — who owns the load: the heaviest database users and client machines/programs (two small tables are fine here, one per grouping). This is where you attribute the consumption to an application.

9. Top SQL (title stays "Top SQL") — two tables: the RECENTLY-ACTIVE list (last 30 minutes, with users_executing = running right now) and the LIFETIME list. For a load ticket lead with the recent list — users_executing > 0 first, then high per-exec cost; use the lifetime list for chronic offenders and note when a lifetime giant is absent from the recent list (history, not the present). Cross-reference sql_id with the session tables so a heavy session and its statement are named together.

10. Recommendations (Portuguese title: Recomendações) — a numbered list; each item starts with a SHORT BOLD TITLE, then 1-3 sentences: what the data shows → the risk → the concrete action. Separate what is happening NOW (live rates, recently-active SQL) from chronic patterns (cumulative tables); a load ticket is answered by the NOW items. Recommend nothing the data does not support. This tool is READ-ONLY: never emit a command that changes anything; a kill or an ALTER is a suggestion for the DBA to review and run manually, clearly labeled as such.

11. Queries not collected (Portuguese title: Consultas não coletadas) — list each NOT COLLECTED query with its ORA error and likely cause. If none: one line saying all were collected.

Final rules: use exclusively this run's results; on RAC always name the instance; distinguish LIVE-RATE from CUMULATIVE figures every time; cite real inst:sid, users, machines and sql_id; recommend nothing without evidence; professional, direct, didactic tone.

sqls.name: Instance — Load Overview
sqls.description: [1] One row per RAC instance: user sessions, active user sessions, CPU count and OS run-queue LOAD. The first place to look on RAC — which NODE is hot. LOAD may be empty on some platforms.
sqls.sql:
SELECT i.inst_id,
       i.instance_name,
       i.host_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gv$session s
         WHERE s.inst_id = i.inst_id AND s.type = 'USER') user_sessions,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gv$session s
         WHERE s.inst_id = i.inst_id AND s.type = 'USER'
           AND s.status = 'ACTIVE') active_user_sessions,
       (SELECT o.value FROM gv$osstat o
         WHERE o.inst_id = i.inst_id AND o.stat_name = 'NUM_CPUS') num_cpus,
       (SELECT ROUND(o.value, 2) FROM gv$osstat o
         WHERE o.inst_id = i.inst_id AND o.stat_name = 'LOAD') os_load
  FROM gv$instance i
 ORDER BY i.inst_id;

sqls.name: Instance — Live Rates (last 60s)
sqls.description: [1] LIVE rates over the last ~60 seconds, not since startup: host CPU %, DB CPU per second, average active sessions, logical reads/s, physical read/write MB/s, network MB/s, OS load. For a 'server is slow NOW' ticket read this FIRST: it is the present measured as a rate, no sampling needed. The scope column says the source: instance-wide gv$sysmetric, or this container's gv$con_sysmetric when connected to a PDB (there the host CPU and OS load rows do not exist — they are instance-scope only).
sqls.sql:
WITH wanted AS (
  SELECT column_value metric_name FROM TABLE(sys.odcivarchar2list(
         'Host CPU Utilization (%)', 'CPU Usage Per Sec',
         'Average Active Sessions', 'Database Time Per Sec',
         'Logical Reads Per Sec', 'Physical Read Total Bytes Per Sec',
         'Physical Write Total Bytes Per Sec',
         'Network Traffic Volume Per Sec', 'Current OS Load'))
), sysm AS (
  SELECT m.inst_id, m.metric_name, m.value, m.metric_unit,
         'instance (gv$sysmetric)' scope
    FROM gv$sysmetric m
    JOIN wanted w ON w.metric_name = m.metric_name
   WHERE m.group_id = 2
), conm AS (
  SELECT m.inst_id, m.metric_name, m.value, m.metric_unit,
         'this container (gv$con_sysmetric)' scope
    FROM gv$con_sysmetric m
    JOIN wanted w ON w.metric_name = m.metric_name
), best AS (
  SELECT * FROM sysm
  UNION ALL
  SELECT * FROM conm WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sysm)
)
SELECT inst_id,
       metric_name,
       CASE WHEN metric_unit LIKE 'Bytes%'
            THEN ROUND(value / 1048576, 2)
            ELSE ROUND(value, 2) END value,
       CASE WHEN metric_unit LIKE 'Bytes%'
            THEN 'MB' || SUBSTR(metric_unit, 6)
            ELSE metric_unit END unit,
       scope
  FROM best
 ORDER BY inst_id, metric_name;

sqls.name: Load — Active Sessions by Wait Class
sqls.description: [1] What the ACTIVE user sessions are doing RIGHT NOW, grouped per instance by resource class. ON CPU is decided by STATE (truly running, not in a wait); sessions that are ACTIVE but parked in an Idle-class wait (job-queue slaves and the like) are excluded. This is the live picture; the resource tables below are cumulative history.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       CASE WHEN s.state != 'WAITING' THEN 'ON CPU'
            ELSE NVL(s.wait_class, 'Other') END resource_class,
       COUNT(*) active_sessions
  FROM gv$session s
 WHERE s.status = 'ACTIVE' AND s.type = 'USER'
   AND NOT (s.state = 'WAITING' AND s.wait_class = 'Idle')
 GROUP BY s.inst_id,
       CASE WHEN s.state != 'WAITING' THEN 'ON CPU'
            ELSE NVL(s.wait_class, 'Other') END
 ORDER BY s.inst_id, active_sessions DESC;

sqls.name: Load — Active Sessions Detail
sqls.description: [1] Every truly ACTIVE user session at collection time (ACTIVE-but-idle waiters excluded): what it runs (sql_id, and since WHEN — sql_running_since is the current statement's execution start), its wait, and its current PGA. Names who is busy NOW; an old sql_running_since = a statement stuck or grinding for that long.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.sql_id,
       TO_CHAR(s.sql_exec_start, 'HH24:MI:SS') sql_running_since,
       s.event,
       s.wait_class,
       s.seconds_in_wait,
       s.last_call_et,
       ROUND(p.pga_alloc_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_alloc_mb
  FROM gv$session s
  LEFT JOIN gv$process p ON p.inst_id = s.inst_id AND p.addr = s.paddr
 WHERE s.status = 'ACTIVE' AND s.type = 'USER'
   AND NOT (s.state = 'WAITING' AND s.wait_class = 'Idle')
 ORDER BY p.pga_alloc_mem DESC NULLS LAST;

sqls.name: Top Sessions — Live Rates (last 15s)
sqls.description: [2] Per-session LIVE rates from gv$sessmetric — work done in the last ~15-second interval only (interval_seconds shows the window): CPU seconds, logical reads, physical read MB and current PGA, with the session's current sql_id. THIS table names who is loading the machine right now; a session huge in the cumulative tables but absent here is not the current problem. EMPTY when connected to a PDB: Oracle populates per-session metrics only at instance scope (CDB root or non-CDB) — then read the active-sessions snapshot and the recently-active Top SQL instead.
sqls.sql:
SELECT sm.inst_id,
       sm.session_id sid,
       sm.serial_num serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.status,
       s.sql_id,
       ROUND(sm.cpu / 100, 2) cpu_seconds,
       sm.logical_reads,
       ROUND(sm.physical_reads
             * (SELECT value FROM v$parameter WHERE name = 'db_block_size')
             / 1048576, 1) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(sm.pga_memory / 1048576, 1) pga_mb,
       ROUND(sm.intsize_csec / 100) interval_seconds
  FROM gv$sessmetric sm
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = sm.inst_id AND s.sid = sm.session_id
                   AND s.serial# = sm.serial_num
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND (sm.cpu > 0 OR sm.logical_reads > 0 OR sm.physical_reads > 0)
 ORDER BY sm.cpu DESC
 FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Session Resource Profile (top by CPU)
sqls.description: [3] The main cumulative table: one row per session with CPU seconds, logical reads, disk read/write MB and SQL*Net MB, top 30 by CPU. CUMULATIVE SINCE LOGON — a long-lived session outranks a briefly-heavy one; cross-check the live-rate tables for who is heavy NOW. The app's table is sortable, so re-rank by any column.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100, 1) cpu_seconds,
       MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_write_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_recv_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes', 'physical write bytes',
                   'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client',
                   'bytes received via SQL*Net from client')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Memory (PGA)
sqls.description: [4] Sessions by CURRENT PGA (used / allocated / max), from gv$process. This one is live, not cumulative. Large pga_alloc_mb = sorts/hashes/PL-SQL collections in memory; pga_max_mb well above alloc = a past spike.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.status,
       ROUND(p.pga_used_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_used_mb,
       ROUND(p.pga_alloc_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_alloc_mb,
       ROUND(p.pga_max_mem / 1048576, 1) pga_max_mb,
       s.sql_id
  FROM gv$session s
  JOIN gv$process p ON p.inst_id = s.inst_id AND p.addr = s.paddr
 WHERE s.type = 'USER' AND p.pga_alloc_mem > 0
 ORDER BY p.pga_alloc_mem DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Instance — PGA Overview
sqls.description: [4] Per-instance PGA aggregate, cumulative SINCE INSTANCE STARTUP: target, allocated, in use, max, over-allocation count, cache hit % and bytes processed vs extra (spill) bytes. over allocation count = times the target had to be EXCEEDED (untunable demand) — NOT a temp-spill counter; actual spill is the extra bytes read/written.
sqls.sql:
SELECT p.inst_id,
       p.name,
       CASE WHEN p.unit = 'bytes' THEN ROUND(p.value / 1048576, 1)
            ELSE p.value END value,
       CASE WHEN p.unit = 'bytes' THEN 'MB' ELSE p.unit END unit
  FROM gv$pgastat p
 WHERE p.name IN ('aggregate PGA target parameter', 'total PGA allocated',
                  'total PGA inuse', 'maximum PGA allocated',
                  'over allocation count', 'cache hit percentage',
                  'bytes processed', 'extra bytes read/written')
 ORDER BY p.inst_id, p.name;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Disk I/O
sqls.description: [5] Sessions by physical read + write MB (real disk traffic), cumulative since logon. The disk consumers; pair with Top SQL to find what they run.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_write_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('physical read bytes', 'physical write bytes')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes' THEN st.value END)
     + MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical write bytes' THEN st.value END) > 0
 ORDER BY phys_read_mb + phys_write_mb DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Logical Reads
sqls.description: [6] Sessions by session logical reads (buffer gets) — CPU and buffer-cache pressure even when data is cached (no disk). A huge logical-read session often means a bad plan doing nested-loop re-reads.
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       st.value logical_reads
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name = 'session logical reads'
   AND st.value > 0
 ORDER BY st.value DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top Sessions by Network (SQL*Net)
sqls.description: [7] Sessions by SQL*Net bytes sent to + received from the client, cumulative. High sent MB = a session shipping huge result sets (missing filter/pagination, array fetch off).
sqls.sql:
SELECT st.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_recv_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('bytes sent via SQL*Net to client',
                   'bytes received via SQL*Net from client')
 GROUP BY st.inst_id, s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.machine, s.program
HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client' THEN st.value END)
     + MAX(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes received via SQL*Net from client' THEN st.value END) > 0
 ORDER BY net_sent_mb + net_recv_mb DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Resource Usage by User
sqls.description: [8] The same resources aggregated per database USER across all instances (sessions, CPU, logical reads, disk MB, network MB). Which application account owns the load. Cumulative.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.username,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid) sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id) on_instances,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576, 1) net_sent_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes', 'bytes sent via SQL*Net to client')
 GROUP BY s.username
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST;

sqls.name: Resource Usage by Machine / Program
sqls.description: [8] Resources aggregated per client machine + program — identifies the app server or tool driving the consumption. Cumulative.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.machine,
       s.program,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid) sessions,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'CPU used by this session'
                      THEN st.value END) / 100) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'session logical reads'
               THEN st.value END) logical_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN sn.name = 'physical read bytes'
                      THEN st.value END) / 1048576) phys_read_mb
  FROM gv$sesstat st
  JOIN gv$statname sn ON sn.inst_id = st.inst_id
                     AND sn.statistic# = st.statistic#
  JOIN gv$session s ON s.inst_id = st.inst_id AND s.sid = st.sid
 WHERE s.type = 'USER'
   AND sn.name IN ('CPU used by this session', 'session logical reads',
                   'physical read bytes')
 GROUP BY s.machine, s.program
 ORDER BY cpu_seconds DESC NULLS LAST
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top SQL — Active in the Last 30 Minutes
sqls.description: [9] The heaviest SQL that EXECUTED in the last 30 minutes (gv$sql filtered by last_active_time), with users_executing = sessions running it RIGHT NOW. For a load ticket lead with users_executing > 0 and high per-exec cost. The totals are still lifetime (since the cursor loaded): recency means the statement ran recently, not that all its cost is recent.
sqls.sql:
SELECT sql_id,
       SUM(users_executing) users_executing,
       TO_CHAR(MAX(last_active_time), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS') last_active,
       SUM(executions) executions,
       ROUND(SUM(elapsed_time) / 1000000, 1) elapsed_seconds,
       ROUND(SUM(cpu_time) / 1000000, 1) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(buffer_gets) buffer_gets,
       SUM(disk_reads) disk_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(buffer_gets) / GREATEST(SUM(executions), 1)) gets_per_exec,
       MAX(parsing_schema_name) parsing_schema,
       MAX(SUBSTR(sql_text, 1, 120)) sql_text
  FROM gv$sql
 WHERE last_active_time >= SYSDATE - INTERVAL '30' MINUTE
 GROUP BY sql_id
HAVING SUM(elapsed_time) > 0
 ORDER BY SUM(elapsed_time) DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;

sqls.name: Top SQL by Resource
sqls.description: [9] The heaviest SQL in the shared pool since each cursor loaded (lifetime totals) — the long-term view to compare against the recently-active list. A giant here that is absent from the recent list is history, not the current load. Match sql_id with the session tables.
sqls.sql:
SELECT sql_id,
       SUM(executions) executions,
       ROUND(SUM(elapsed_time) / 1000000, 1) elapsed_seconds,
       ROUND(SUM(cpu_time) / 1000000, 1) cpu_seconds,
       SUM(buffer_gets) buffer_gets,
       SUM(disk_reads) disk_reads,
       ROUND(SUM(buffer_gets) / GREATEST(SUM(executions), 1)) gets_per_exec,
       MAX(parsing_schema_name) parsing_schema,
       MAX(SUBSTR(sql_text, 1, 120)) sql_text
  FROM gv$sql
 GROUP BY sql_id
HAVING SUM(elapsed_time) > 0
 ORDER BY SUM(elapsed_time) DESC
 FETCH FIRST 30 ROWS ONLY;
